content: {"summary":"Increasing maximumPoolSize during the incident is not recommended. Evidence shows the CPU rise was a by‑product while the Hikari pool was fully used because the reconciliation batch ran with more parallel workers than available connections. The team resolved it by throttling the batch, not by enlarging the pool, and guidance warns that raising the pool merely masks the problem.","likely_cause":"Reconciliation batch parallelism (LEDGER_RECON_PARALLELISM) exceeded the HikariCP maximumPoolSize, exhausting all connections and causing pending requests.","confidence":"high","claims":[{"text":"CPU climb was not the root cause; pool exhaustion drove the failure.","evidence_ids":["RB-013#2"],"quote":"CPU on that pod was clearly elevated, around two thirds of its limit, but it never got close to the limit."},{"text":"Batch parallelism was higher than the pool size, filling all connections.","evidence_ids":["RB-013#5"],"quote":"The batch's parallelism was LEDGER_RECON_PARALLELISM=24, more workers than the pool has connections."},{"text":"The incident was resolved without changing maximumPoolSize.","evidence_ids":["RB-013#6"],"quote":"We did not raise maximumPoolSize."},{"text":"Raising the pool only hides the underlying connection pressure.","evidence_ids":["RB-010#6"],"quote":"Raising pool hides the problem and moves pressure to payments-pgbouncer."}],"next_checks":["Monitor hikaricp_connections_pending and active connections during batch runs","Check thread dumps for HikariPool.getConnection stacks to confirm which threads hold connections","Verify and, if needed, lower LEDGER_RECON_PARALLELISM during high‑load periods","Consider configuring a separate Hikari pool for the reconciliation batch"]}
